Transcript body (timestamps approximate):
[00:00] Lina (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking time. Quick intros — I'm Lina, AE at Redwood. Marco is our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Sasha (Borealis): Sasha here, CTO. Thanks, Lina. Devon and Priya from my team are on as well, and Ethan.
[00:18] Marco (Redwood SE): Hi all. Quick agenda — understand Borealis's integration surface, security constraints, and propose pilot approach.
[00:28] Devon (Borealis): High level — Borealis runs a multi-tenant SaaS analytics product for financial customers. We do model-assisted summarization and semantic search on customer data; latency matters at 95th. We're evaluating connectors to vendor inference platforms—looking for predictable cost and ability to route sensitive customers to on-prem or VPC.
[00:45] Lina: Great. Can you share current stack? Are you self-hosting models today or using a cloud provider?
[00:52] Ethan (Borealis): We have a mix — some inference runs on GCP endpoints (managed), some on in-house NVIDIA A100 boxes. But ops is heavy and cost is spiky. We want a managed partner to offload infra, but must keep ability to isolate certain high-risk tenants on-prem.
[01:10] Priya (Borealis): From security side, we need SOC 2 Type II evidence, customer-tenant isolation guarantees, KMS/HSM support for encryption keys, and audit log retention for 1 year. Also, data-at-rest residency in EU for certain customers.
[01:28] Marco: Understood. Redwood has hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private VPC/on-prem options that map to those needs. For KMS — we support customer-managed KMS keys in Private and Dedicated; hosted has envelope encryption and we can discuss bring-your-own-key for enterprise. Audit logs and retention are part of our console add-on.
[01:50] Sasha: Can you explain the routing/fallback strategy? If a region is out of capacity, what happens to requests pinned to a dedicated pool?
[01:58] Marco: Good question. We support policy-based routing — you can pin by tenant, model version, or latency tier. For dedicated pools we recommend autoscaling and burst policies; if capacity is exhausted, policy options are: queue (not ideal), failover to a compatible model variant in hosted with masking, or reroute to another region with consent.
[02:22] Sasha: Masking?
[02:24] Marco: Meaning we can run the request through a less costly quantized variant or a smaller model that preserves semantics but may degrade generation length. It's a configurable fallback.
[02:33] Devon: That degradation is risky for our summarization accuracy metric. How do you measure quality regression?
[02:39] Lina: We tie quality monitoring to evals and prompt sets. As part of Redwood Optimize we automatically run a prompt suite on both primary and fallback models and alert on regression thresholds. You can set rollbacks.
[02:50] Priya: About audit logs — what granularity? We need token-level usage per tenant and per-route.
[02:57] Marco: We can provide token-level billing and latency traces per route, with request/response metadata. Note full PII in payloads won't be stored if you enable redaction hooks; we provide a middleware to redact before logging.
[03:12] Sasha: Cost — primary driver. We need ballpark unit economics vs our current self-hosted A100 fleet.
[03:20] Lina: Pricing will vary by model and whether it's hosted or dedicated. Generally dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable per-token cost; hosted is variable but no infra ops. For pilot, we'll do a cost projection using your QPS and token distribution. Marco will formalize the mini-benchmark to compare p95 latencies and cost per 1M tokens.
[03:39] Ethan: About hybrid — we want to keep customer A's data fully on-prem; others can go to hosted. How does Redwood handle multi-tenant routing?
[03:48] Marco: You can route per-tenant via headers and our routing policy engine. For on-prem, you'd run Redwood Private control plane and attach private workers in your VPC or data center; requests from tenant A can be route-local. For SaaS customers, we also support 'edge onramps' — a small connector that forwards encrypted traffic to your private pool.
[04:10] Devon: SDKs? We want language SDKs and server SDK for our backend.
[04:15] Lina: We have REST + multi-language SDKs, and detailed server-side examples for connectors.
[04:19] [04:19] (microphone hiss / brief cross-talk)
[04:28] Priya: Can you do certs for data residency? We need EU data to remain in EU.
[04:33] Marco: Yes, region pinning is supported. For hosted we operate regions in EU and NA; for sensitive customers we recommend private deployment inside your EU cloud or on-prem.
[04:40] Sasha: Let's drill into perf — our 95th p95 tail needs to be below 500ms for short prompts, and long summaries are allowed to be slower but p95 ideally under 2s. What latency do you see on similar workloads?
[04:53] Marco: Depends on model size and sequence lengths. For medium-sized models on T4/A10 style instances we typically see 150–400ms p95 for short prompts with continuous batching tuned; with A100-ish hardware and kernel optimizations you can get sub-200ms for many workloads. We'll benchmark with your prompt mix.
[05:14] Devon: How about concurrency and batching — we have bursty traffic around market opens. Can autoscaling cover that without huge cost?
[05:22] Lina: Autoscaling and burst pools help. Also KV/prefix caching reduces tokens for repeated context in chat-like summarization. Our Optimize tooling suggests batching windows to balance latency and cost. For very spiky QPS you might use a small dedicated pool plus hosted burst fallback — policy-based.
[05:43] Priya: HSM/KMS specifics — we need FIPS 140-2 compliant key management and the ability for our security team to rotate keys.
[05:52] Marco: In Private and Dedicated, you can bring your own KMS or HSM. We integrate with common cloud KMS providers and support HSM in on-prem setups. Key rotation is supported; logs show key usage. For hosted, we have envelope encryption but can discuss additional enterprise contracts for BYOK.
[06:12] Sasha: Any blind spots — are there limitations with large KV caches or sequence lengths?
[06:18] Marco: Very long sequence lengths can impact memory and cost; our runtime handles KV cache eviction and continuous batching, but you need to tune cache sizes. For very large context windows we recommend quantized model variants or model sharding in private deployments.
[06:33] Ethan: For the pilot — what's realistic? Two weeks? We want production-like traffic replay.
[06:38] Lina: Two-week pilot is reasonable. We'll do a scoped benchmark: replay of representative traffic (anonymized), p95/p99 latency, token cost, and a quality check on 200 labeled prompts. Marco will own bench plan.
[06:50] Marco: I'll include checklist: required access, sample prompts, traffic histogram, target SLOs, and a small runbook for on-prem connector install. Also will note any config for VPC peering or VPN.
[07:04] Devon: VPN/peering complexity — can you support a temporary connector instead of full VPC peering for pilot?
[07:09] Marco: Yes, for pilot we can use an outbound-only connector with mutual TLS, which is lighter. Production on-prem usually transitions to VPC peering or direct connect.
[07:20] Priya: What about data retention for logs? If logs must be retained for a year, that increases storage cost. Does Redwood provide tiered retention?
[07:29] Marco: Yes, retention is configurable per-route — you can set 30/90/365 days. We charge additional for long-term retention but can scope this in the pricing proposal.
[07:40] Sasha: Any legal or procurement blockers you usually see for partners like us?
[07:46] Lina: Standard items: DPA, security questionnaire (SIG), sometimes specific SLAs for p95 latency. We'll surface the base contract and addenda for private deployments.
[07:57] Ethan: Onboarding timeline — assuming pilot OK, how long to stand up dedicated pool?
[08:02] Marco: Dedicated reserved pool provisioning takes about 1–2 weeks once capacity is committed. Private on-prem can be longer depending on network/setup, maybe 3–6 weeks.
[08:12] Devon: Can we do an initial hosted pilot and then move workloads to dedicated if cost analysis favors it?
[08:17] Lina: Yes, that's common. We can start hosted, measure, then reserve capacity and migrate routes with minimal change to your code—routing rules are declarative.
[08:27] Sasha: A few clarifying Qs on failure modes: If fallback to hosted from dedicated happens, are there billing anomalies or separate metering?
[08:36] Marco: Fallback will be metered as hosted usage unless included in committed burst terms. We'll show per-route metering so you can attribute cost.
[08:45] Lina: Quick note — we have a short deck that explains deployment patterns and a security pack. I'll drop links in the follow-up.
[08:52] Priya: Please include the SOC2 report redaction and list of sub-processors. That's key for legal.
[08:59] Lina: Noted.
[09:02] (brief pause / typing)
[09:12] Sasha: Anything else we should know about quantization and hallucination risk?
[09:17] Marco: Quantization can affect perplexity and sometimes subtle behaviours; we recommend running quality evals. For hallucination-sensitive outputs we may keep larger variants for those routes and use quantized for lower-risk tasks. Redwood Optimize suggests per-route quant profiles.
[09:33] Devon: Operationally, how do we test rollbacks if a new model version regresses?
[09:38] Marco: You can do canary rollouts and automatic rollback based on the prompt-suite evaluation, plus traffic-based heuristics. The console exposes diffing and repro steps.
[09:49] Sasha: Let's wrap with immediate asks and owners.
[09:52] Lina: Sure. Quick recap: Marco will send benchmark plan; I'll send security/compliance pack, contract starter and deployment patterns deck; Ethan will send sample traffic and prompt set. We aim to start pilot week of 2029-12-02 pending paperwork.
[10:10] Priya: Timeline okay. Also, can you include a short note about data redaction hooks?
[10:15] Marco: Yes, will include sample middleware and code snippets.
[10:19] Sasha: Great. Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[10:23] Lina: Thanks — we'll follow up in email.
